reading.body:
Georgia's 2025 and 2026 legislative sessions produced 105 AI-related bills, and the largest single cluster is not about AI models at all. It is about data centers, electricity, and who pays for them.

Nine bills in this list target data center power and cost directly. SB34 would bar electric utilities from recovering the cost of serving commercial data centers through rates. HB1063 would protect residential and retail customers from data center construction and operation costs. HB1323 would require new data centers to operate as hybrid power data centers. HB1059 would impose a moratorium on data center development, and HB1012 would prohibit local governments from approving new data centers for a set period. SB421 and SB436 push transparency in the other direction, requiring disclosure of data center electricity and water use and barring local governments from signing nondisclosure agreements about it. Three more bills, SB408, SB410, and HB559, touch the data center equipment sales and use tax exemption, with two advancing its sunset and one repealing it. HB1387 ties a homestead exemption to revenue collected from taxing data centers. That is a state legislature treating compute infrastructure as a utility-scale land use question, not a technology question.

The second pattern is that Georgia is legislating AI's outputs and its inputs at the same time, without a unifying framework. On outputs: SB540 would require disclosures for conversational AI services, HB478 would require disclaimers on AI-generated content, HB1603 and HB1399 address performer likeness and generative AI in entertainment, and SB488 would make generative AI systems personal property for product liability suits involving minors. On inputs: the data center bills above. On process: SR789, HR1788, SB455, SR391, SR431, and HR815 would create study committees or a commission on AI, and HB147 and HB1351 would require state agencies to inventory or disclose their AI use. The volume is high and the scope is scattered, which is what early-stage legislation looks like before a state settles on a regulatory model.

What the data does not show is enactment. These are bill records with dates, and the list includes commendations and study committee resolutions alongside substantive bills. Nothing here establishes which measures passed, which died, or what any of them cost. It also does not cover local ordinances, utility commission proceedings, or the private power contracts that determine whether a data center in Georgia actually gets built. The reader should treat this as a map of legislative attention, not of law.

The data center bills split into two mechanisms that are easy to conflate. One group shifts cost: SB34, HB1063, and HB1387 all try to move money between ratepayers, taxpayers, and data center operators. The other group shifts information: SB421, SB436, and HB1059 try to make electricity and water use visible or to stop construction outright. Cost-shifting bills need a ratemaking body to act on them. Information bills can change outcomes on their own, because a disclosed load figure is what a county commission or a utility uses in the next proceeding. The transparency bills are the cheaper lever and the harder one to reverse.

The dates show the sequence. The earliest data center measures in this list are SB34 and HB559 in January and February 2025, both about who pays and what is exempt. The moratorium and transparency bills arrive later, HB1012 and SB421 in January 2026, HB1059 in January 2026. Cost questions came first, and land use and disclosure questions followed. That order is what you would expect if legislators learned the size of the load after the tax exemption was already in place.

Georgia also has more AI study bodies than AI enforcement bodies in this data. SR789, HR1788, SB455, SR391, SR431, and HR815 would create committees or a commission. SB9, SB37, and SB167 are the bills that would create actual duties or causes of action. A study committee produces a report, and a report is the input to a bill in the following session. The 2026 committee bills are therefore a leading indicator for 2027 legislation, not a substitute for it.

What is the data center equipment sales and use tax exemption and why are there three bills about it?
The data does not describe the exemption's terms or value. Three bills reference it: SB408 would advance its sunset date, SB410 would repeal it, and HB559 would revise its sunset date. All three were introduced in 2025, and the data does not show which, if any, took effect.

Which Georgia AI bills actually became law?
The data does not hold this. It contains bill numbers, titles, and dates only, with no status field, so enactment cannot be determined from it.

Why does a state with a study committee on AI also have a moratorium on data centers?
The data does not state a reason. It shows both exist in the same two sessions, with the study committee resolutions and the data center bills filed by different chambers and sponsors. The two tracks address different questions: how the state should govern AI, and whether it can power it.

What would SB34 and HB1063 do to electricity rates for data centers?
Both would keep data center costs out of what residential and retail customers pay. SB34 would prohibit including a utility's data center service costs in rates, and HB1063 would protect residential and retail customers from data center construction and operation costs. The data does not show the rates, the cost figures, or the outcome of either bill.

Which bills in this list address AI in hiring or employment?
HB1351 would require state agencies to notify employees when using AI in personnel matters. SB167 would require private entities using certain AI systems to guard against discrimination caused by those systems. No other bill in the list addresses employment uses of AI.

How many of these bills are about AI at all, versus data centers or something else?
The list is a set of 105 records, and many titles do not mention AI, including tax, education, health, and commendation measures. The data does not include a category field, so a precise count of AI-specific bills cannot be derived from it.
